worlds.title: Data Types & Variables
worlds.theme: The mainframe is cold. Power up its cores and route the raw signals pouring in from the grid.

worlds.title: Control Flow & Logic
worlds.theme: Every packet hits a fork. Teach the matrix to pick routes, filter junk data and run security checks.

worlds.title: Data Structures
worlds.theme: Payloads, sensor logs and entity records are piling up in the vaults. Parse them before they overflow.

worlds.title: Loops & Iteration
worlds.theme: Manual work doesn't scale. Spin up engines that batch-process records and retry failed links on their own.

worlds.title: Functions & Scope
worlds.theme: Package your logic into reusable engine modules and API handlers the whole grid can call.

levels.title: Power On
levels.briefing: Operator, the mainframe is dark. Its boot checklist needs four readings stored in named registers before the cores will spin up.
levels.objective: Create status (text ONLINE), active_cores (whole number 4), core_temp (decimal 36.6) and shields_up (True). Then print status.
levels.starterCode:
# Mainframe boot checklist
# status       -> the text ONLINE
# active_cores -> the whole number 4
# core_temp    -> the decimal 36.6
# shields_up   -> the boolean True
# Finally, print status.
levels.solution:
status = "ONLINE"
active_cores = 4
core_temp = 36.6
shields_up = True
print(status)

tests.label: active_cores is an int
tests.name: active_cores
tests.failHint: Write 4 without quotes or a decimal point.

tests.label: shields_up is True
tests.name: shields_up
tests.failHint: Booleans are True / False with a capital letter and no quotes.

hints: A variable is a name, an equals sign, and a value: name = value.
Text goes in quotes ("ONLINE"), numbers don't (4, 36.6), and booleans are written True or False.
print(status) prints the value stored in status — no quotes around the name.

careers.dataScience: Every DataFrame column has a dtype (int64, float64, bool, object). Choosing the right one controls memory use and which maths is allowed.
careers.softwareEngineering: Config flags, counters and thresholds are typed variables. Type hints like `retries: int` start right here.
careers.webDevelopment: Request params arrive as strings, but your database expects ints and bools. Knowing the core types is the first step in validating input.

levels.title: Signal Converter
levels.concept: Type casting with int() and str()
levels.briefing: The antenna sends raw_signal as TEXT. The booster adds 8 to it, but you can't add a number to text. Repair the converter.
levels.objective: Fill the blanks so the text signal becomes a number, gets boosted, and is printed as part of a message.

tests.label: Prints "Signal strength: 50"
tests.failHint: float() would give 50.0 — the spec wants a whole number.

hints: "42" + 8 is an error: text and numbers don't mix with +.
int("42") turns text into the number 42. str(50) turns a number back into text "50".

careers.dataScience: CSV columns often load as strings. `df["price"].astype(float)` is the same casting idea at scale.
careers.softwareEngineering: Parsing env vars and CLI args means casting: `int(os.environ["PORT"])`.
careers.webDevelopment: Query strings like ?page=2 always arrive as text. Cast before you do arithmetic or database lookups.

levels.title: Telemetry Readout
levels.briefing: A junior operator multiplied a voltage reading and the dashboard went haywire. Predict what the console showed.
levels.objective: What does this program print?
levels.explanation: voltage is the TEXT "12", not the number 12. Multiplying a string by an int repeats it: "12" * 3 == "121212". Use int(voltage) * 3 to get 36.
hints: Look closely at the quotes on line 1.
For strings, * means "repeat" — try "ab" * 2 in your head.

careers.dataScience: A numeric column silently loaded as text will 'multiply' into nonsense. Always check dtypes after loading data.
careers.softwareEngineering: Operator overloading: + and * mean different things for str, list and int. Knowing this prevents subtle bugs.
careers.webDevelopment: Form values are strings. "5" * 2 giving "55" is a classic checkout-total bug.

levels.title: Packet Loss Ratio
levels.briefing: The relay reports how many packets it sent and lost, but as TEXT. Command wants the loss rate as a percentage, rounded to 2 decimals.
levels.objective: Convert packets_sent and packets_lost to numbers, compute loss_rate = lost / sent * 100 rounded to 2 places, and print: Loss rate: <loss_rate>%
levels.starterCode:
# Sensor inputs (TEXT): packets_sent, packets_lost
# 1. Convert both to int.
# 2. loss_rate = lost / sent * 100, rounded to 2 decimals.
# 3. Print:  Loss rate: <loss_rate>%
levels.solution:
sent = int(packets_sent)
lost = int(packets_lost)
loss_rate = round(lost / sent * 100, 2)
print(f"Loss rate: {loss_rate}%")
hints: int(packets_sent) turns the text into a number you can divide.
round(value, 2) keeps two decimal places.
An f-string mixes text and values: f"Loss rate: {loss_rate}%"

careers.dataScience: Rates and percentages are everyday metrics: conversion rate, churn, error rate. Rounding is for display; keep full precision in calculations.
careers.softwareEngineering: Monitoring dashboards (SLOs, error budgets) compute exactly this kind of ratio from raw counters.
careers.webDevelopment: Formatting numbers for display with f-strings is the backend half of every analytics widget.

levels.title: Route Fork
levels.briefing: A courier drone reports its fuel level. With 50 or more it takes the highway, with 20 or more the backroad, otherwise it must refuel. The router code is damaged.
levels.objective: Repair the decision chain so every fuel level picks the right route.
levels.template:
if fuel {{cmp}} 50:
    route = "highway"
{{elif_kw}} fuel >= 20:
    route = "backroad"
{{else_kw}}:
    route = "refuel"
print("Route:", route)
hints: Python checks the branches top to bottom and runs only the first one that is True.
"Or more" means greater-than-or-equal: >=
Python's "else if" is spelled elif.

careers.dataScience: Binning a value into categories (low / mid / high) is a classic feature-engineering step — pandas' `pd.cut` does it in bulk.
careers.softwareEngineering: Feature flags, retry policies and routing rules are all if/elif chains at heart.
careers.webDevelopment: Choosing which template, redirect or HTTP status to return is control flow in every request handler.

levels.title: Packet Filter
levels.briefing: Junk packets are flooding the matrix. A packet passes only if its size is 64–1500 bytes (inclusive), its checksum is valid, and its source is not "unknown".
levels.objective: Fix the accepted = ... line so it is True only for valid packets.
levels.starterCode:
# Sensor inputs: packet_size (int), checksum_ok (bool), source (str)
# A packet is valid only when ALL of these hold:
#   - packet_size is between 64 and 1500 (inclusive)
#   - checksum_ok is True
#   - source is not "unknown"
accepted = False   # <- fix this line

if accepted:
    print("ACCEPT")
else:
    print("DROP")
hints: and is True only when both sides are True.
Python lets you chain comparisons: 64 <= packet_size <= 1500
"Is not" for values is written != (e.g. source != "unknown").

careers.dataScience: Boolean masks: `df[(df.size >= 64) & (df.ok)]` filters rows with exactly this logic.
careers.softwareEngineering: Guard clauses and input validation combine several conditions before doing any real work.
careers.webDevelopment: Authorization checks: is the user logged in AND the owner AND not banned?

levels.title: Security Clearance
levels.concept: Operator precedence of and / or / not
levels.briefing: An intruder slipped past the checkpoint using a maintenance override. Trace the checkpoint logic to see what it printed.
levels.objective: What does this program print?
levels.explanation: and binds tighter than or, so the condition reads (clearance >= 3 and has_badge) or override → (True and False) or True → False or True → True. The first branch runs. Add parentheses when mixing and/or so the intent is obvious.
hints: Evaluate and before or — like * before +.
Group it as (clearance >= 3 and has_badge) or override.

careers.dataScience: Mis-grouped filters silently include the wrong rows. Parenthesize compound masks.
careers.softwareEngineering: Precedence bugs in permission checks are real security vulnerabilities. Code review catches them; tests prove them.
careers.webDevelopment: Access-control middleware is exactly this logic. An accidental `or` can open an admin route.

levels.title: Threat Level
levels.briefing: The perimeter grid scores threats from 0 to 100. Build the alert classifier. If the sensors are offline, nothing else can be trusted.
levels.objective: Set alert to OFFLINE / RED / AMBER / GREEN by the rules, then print: ALERT: <alert>
levels.starterCode:
# Sensor inputs: threat_score (0-100), sensors_online (bool)
# Rules, checked in this order:
#   sensors offline     -> "OFFLINE"
#   score 70 or higher  -> "RED"
#   score 30 or higher  -> "AMBER"
#   anything else       -> "GREEN"
# Store the result in alert, then print:  ALERT: <alert>

tests.label: 70 → RED
tests.failHint: Check RED before AMBER — 70 is also >= 30.

hints: Order matters: the first True branch wins, so test the most specific rule first.
not sensors_online is True when the sensors are offline.
Shape: if ... / elif ... / elif ... / else.

careers.dataScience: Rule-based labelling (risk tiers, customer segments) is often the baseline a model has to beat.
careers.softwareEngineering: Alert severities in monitoring tools like PagerDuty follow ordered threshold rules exactly like this.
careers.webDevelopment: Rendering status badges (success / warning / danger) from a numeric score.

levels.title: Payload Parser
levels.briefing: Sensor readings arrive as a list, oldest first. The parser needs the first reading, the latest one, and the three most recent — and lists come in all lengths.
levels.objective: Fill in the indexes so the parser works for a list of any length.
levels.template:
first = readings[{{first}}]
latest = readings[{{last}}]
recent = readings[{{tail}}]
print("first:", first, "| latest:", latest, "| recent:", recent)

tests.label: latest works for 7 readings
tests.name: latest
tests.failHint: Hard-coded positions break when the list grows. Negative indexes count from the end.

hints: Indexes start at 0, so the first item is readings[0].
Negative indexes count from the end: readings[-1] is the last item.
A slice readings[-3:] means "from the third-from-last to the end".

careers.dataScience: `df.head()`, `df.tail(3)` and `series.iloc[-1]` are indexing and slicing on steroids.
careers.softwareEngineering: Ring buffers, log tails and pagination all rely on slicing the most recent N items.
careers.webDevelopment: "Show the 3 latest posts" is posts[-3:] (or a LIMIT in SQL).

levels.title: Entity Records
levels.briefing: An operator record has landed in the vault as a dictionary. Read it, promote the operator to admin, flag them active, and safely read an email that may not exist.
levels.objective: username = the name, set role to "admin", add active = True, email = the email or "none" if missing, then print: <username> -> <role>
levels.starterCode:
# Sensor input: user (a dict), e.g. {"id": 7, "name": "ada", "role": "analyst"}
# 1. username = the user's name
# 2. change the user's role to "admin"
# 3. add a key "active" with the value True
# 4. email = the user's email, or "none" if there isn't one (no crashing!)
# 5. print:  <username> -> <role>
levels.solution:
username = user["name"]
user["role"] = "admin"
user["active"] = True
email = user.get("email", "none")
print(f"{username} -> {user['role']}")

tests.label: Missing email becomes "none"
tests.name: email
tests.failHint: user["email"] crashes when the key is missing. .get() takes a fallback.

hints: Read a value with d["key"]; write one with d["key"] = value.
Assigning to a key that doesn't exist yet adds it.
d.get("key", fallback) returns fallback instead of raising KeyError.

careers.dataScience: JSON records from APIs become dicts; a list of dicts becomes a DataFrame with `pd.DataFrame(records)`.
careers.softwareEngineering: Dicts are Python's hash maps: caches, lookup tables and config objects are all dicts.
careers.webDevelopment: Request bodies and JSON responses are dicts. `.get()` with a default stops optional fields from crashing your API.

levels.title: Sector Scan
levels.briefing: A scanner logged the sectors it swept as a tuple. Analytics converted it to a set. Predict the report line.
levels.objective: What does this program print?
levels.snippet:
sweep = (3, 7, 3, 9)
unique = set(sweep)
print(len(sweep), len(unique), sweep.count(3))
levels.explanation: A tuple keeps every item in order, duplicates included, so len(sweep) is 4 and sweep.count(3) is 2. A set keeps only unique values — {3, 7, 9} — so len(unique) is 3.
hints: Tuples keep duplicates. Sets drop them.
.count(x) counts how many times x appears.

careers.dataScience: `series.nunique()` and `value_counts()` are set and count logic for whole columns.
careers.softwareEngineering: Tuples are immutable records (great dict keys). Sets give O(1) membership tests for de-duplication.
careers.webDevelopment: De-duplicating tags, or checking whether a permission is in a user's set of roles.

levels.title: Sensor Dedup
levels.briefing: Two monitoring stations sent overlapping sensor logs, with duplicates. Find which sensors both stations saw, the full roster, and pack a summary tuple.
levels.objective: shared = sensors in both logs, all_ids = sensors in either, report = (number shared, number total). Print: <total> unique sensors, <shared> shared
levels.starterCode:
# Sensor inputs: log_a, log_b (lists of sensor ids, may contain duplicates)
# shared  -> a set of ids that appear in BOTH logs
# all_ids -> a set of ids that appear in EITHER log
# report  -> a tuple: (how many shared, how many in total)
# print:  <total> unique sensors, <shared> shared
levels.solution:
shared = set(log_a) & set(log_b)
all_ids = set(log_a) | set(log_b)
report = (len(shared), len(all_ids))
print(f"{report[1]} unique sensors, {report[0]} shared")

tests.label: Handles logs with nothing in common

hints: set(some_list) removes duplicates.
a & b is the intersection (in both); a | b is the union (in either).
A tuple is written with parentheses: (x, y).

careers.dataScience: Comparing ID sets is how you check join coverage between two datasets before merging.
careers.softwareEngineering: Diffing two inventories (deployed vs desired services) is set algebra.
careers.webDevelopment: Mutual followers, shared tags, or permissions common to two roles — intersection again.

levels.title: Batch Processor
levels.briefing: A batch of transaction records needs totalling. The fancy sum() module is offline — build the accumulator loop by hand.
levels.objective: Loop over records, add each one to total and count how many there are. Don't use sum().
levels.starterCode:
# Sensor input: records (a list of numbers)
total = 0
count = 0
# Loop over records: add each one to total, and count them.

print(f"Processed {count} records, total {total}")
levels.solution:
total = 0
count = 0
for record in records:
    total += record
    count += 1
print(f"Processed {count} records, total {total}")
hints: for record in records: runs the indented block once per item.
Inside the loop: total += record adds to the running total.
count += 1 inside the loop counts iterations.

careers.dataScience: Accumulators are what `.sum()`, `.mean()` and `groupby().agg()` do under the hood — and how you write custom aggregations.
careers.softwareEngineering: Processing queues, files and streams one item at a time is the backbone of ETL jobs and workers.
careers.webDevelopment: Computing a cart total or rendering a list of items means looping over a collection.

levels.title: Retry Mechanism
levels.briefing: The uplink is flaky. Keep retrying until it connects, but give up after 5 attempts. Careful: a broken counter loops forever and overheats the core.
levels.objective: Repair the retry loop. The link succeeds on attempt number success_on.
levels.template:
attempts = 0
connected = False
while {{not_kw}} connected and attempts < 5:
    attempts {{inc}} 1
    if attempts == success_on:
        connected = True
print("attempts:", attempts, "connected:", connected)

tests.label: Gives up after 5 attempts
tests.failHint: The loop must stop when attempts reaches 5.

hints: The loop should keep going while we are NOT connected.
attempts = 1 sets it to 1 every time — the loop never progresses. You need to add to it.
x += 1 is shorthand for x = x + 1.

careers.dataScience: Training loops run while the loss is still improving and epochs < max — the same guard pattern.
careers.softwareEngineering: Retry-with-limit (plus backoff) is standard for network calls; libraries like tenacity wrap exactly this loop.
careers.webDevelopment: Polling an API until a job finishes, with a max-attempts cap so the page never hangs.

levels.title: Signal Skipper
levels.briefing: A filter engine skips even channel codes and shuts down when codes get too high. Predict which channels get broadcast.
levels.objective: What does this program print?
levels.explanation: range(1, 8) yields 1–7. Even codes hit continue and are skipped. Odd codes 1, 3 and 5 are printed. At 7, code > 5 triggers break, so 7 is never printed.
hints: range(1, 8) stops BEFORE 8.
continue jumps to the next iteration; break exits the loop entirely.

careers.dataScience: Skipping invalid rows (continue) and early stopping (break) are everyday patterns in data-cleaning loops.
careers.softwareEngineering: Short-circuiting a search loop with break as soon as you find a match saves work.
careers.webDevelopment: Skipping hidden items while rendering, or stopping pagination at the first empty page.

levels.title: Error Sweep
levels.briefing: The system log is a list of entries. Collect the code of every ERROR entry, but stop the sweep the moment you hit HALT — everything after it is corrupted.
levels.objective: Fill errors with the codes after "ERROR:" (e.g. "ERROR:disk" → "disk"), stopping at "HALT". Use break.
levels.starterCode:
# Sensor input: logs (a list of strings)
errors = []
for entry in logs:
    # 1. If entry is "HALT", stop the sweep immediately.
    # 2. If entry starts with "ERROR:", store the code after the colon.
    #    e.g. "ERROR:disk" -> "disk"
    pass

print(f"{len(errors)} errors found")

tests.label: errors = ["disk", "net"]
tests.name: errors
tests.failHint: Did you stop at HALT? "ghost" comes after it.

hints: Check for HALT first and break out of the loop.
entry.startswith("ERROR:") tells you whether it is an error entry.
"ERROR:" is 6 characters, so entry[6:] is everything after it. Then errors.append(...).

careers.dataScience: Parsing raw logs into structured fields is the first step of most real-world data pipelines.
careers.softwareEngineering: Log scanners and incident tooling filter, extract and stop at sentinel markers just like this.
careers.webDevelopment: Parsing access logs to find failed requests, or processing a stream until an end-of-stream marker.

levels.title: Engine Module
levels.briefing: The thrust calculation is copy-pasted all over the grid. Package it as a reusable module — but the module's keywords got scrambled.
levels.objective: Repair the function so calculate_thrust(mass, acceleration) hands back mass × acceleration.
levels.template:
{{def_kw}} calculate_thrust(mass, acceleration):
    force = mass * acceleration
    {{ret_kw}} force

print(calculate_thrust(1200, 10))

tests.label: Prints 12000
tests.failHint: print shows a value but doesn't hand it back — the caller gets None.

hints: Functions are defined with the def keyword.
return sends a value back to whoever called the function. print only displays it.

careers.dataScience: Reusable functions turn one-off notebook cells into a feature pipeline you can apply to every dataset.
careers.softwareEngineering: Functions are the smallest unit of reuse and testing. Pure functions (input → return) are easiest to test.
careers.webDevelopment: Every route handler and template helper is a function that returns a response or a value.

levels.title: Response Handler
levels.briefing: Every API on the grid must reply in the same envelope. Build the handler that wraps a status code and optional data into a standard response.
levels.objective: build_response(status, data=None) returns {"status": status, "ok": status < 400, "data": data}, using {} when no data is given.

tests.label: An empty list is still data
tests.failHint: `data or {}` replaces ANY falsy value, including []. Check `data is None` instead.

hints: A default parameter (data=None) is used when the caller leaves that argument out.
Use `if data is None:` to detect a missing argument.
status < 400 is already a bool — you can put it straight into the dict.

careers.dataScience: Model-serving endpoints wrap predictions in a consistent envelope so dashboards can parse them.
careers.softwareEngineering: `None` as a default (never a mutable `{}` or `[]`) avoids the infamous shared-default bug.
careers.webDevelopment: This is the JSON envelope pattern used by REST APIs in Flask, FastAPI and Django.

levels.title: Scope Leak
levels.briefing: A module tried to overclock the global power setting from inside a function. Did it actually change? Predict the output.
levels.objective: What does this program print?
levels.snippet:
power = 10

def boost():
    power = 99
    return power + 1

result = boost()
print(result, power)
levels.explanation: Assigning power = 99 inside boost() creates a NEW local variable that only exists inside the function. boost() returns 99 + 1 = 100, and the global power is untouched at 10. Functions should communicate through parameters and return values, not by changing globals.
hints: An assignment inside a function creates a local variable by default.
The global power and the local power are two different variables that share a name.

careers.dataScience: Notebook globals cause 'works on my machine' bugs. Pass data into functions explicitly.
careers.softwareEngineering: Avoiding shared mutable global state makes code testable and thread-safe.
careers.webDevelopment: Request handlers must not keep per-user data in module globals — it leaks between users.

levels.title: API Gatekeeper
levels.briefing: Final system: the sign-up API needs a validator module. It must return every problem it finds, in a fixed order, so the client can show them all at once.
levels.objective: validate_user(payload, strict=False) returns a list of error strings in this order: "invalid email", "invalid age", "missing name" (strict only). Return [] when valid.
levels.starterCode:
# validate_user(payload, strict=False) -> list of error strings, in this order:
#   "invalid email" if "email" is missing or has no "@" in it
#   "invalid age"   if "age" is missing, not an int, or under 13
#   "missing name"  ONLY when strict is True and "name" is missing
# Return an empty list when everything is valid.

def validate_user(payload, strict=False):
    errors = []
    return errors

print(validate_user({"email": "neo@grid.io", "age": 9}))

tests.label: Missing email doesn't crash
tests.failHint: payload["email"] raises KeyError when it's missing — use .get() with a default.

tests.label: Age sent as text
tests.failHint: isinstance(age, int) checks the type before you compare.

hints: Use independent if statements (not elif) — you want to collect ALL errors.
payload.get("email", "") gives an empty string when the key is missing, and "@" not in "" is True.
isinstance(age, int) is False for None and for "30" — check it before comparing with 13.

careers.dataScience: Data-quality checks (schema, ranges, required fields) run before any analysis — tools like Great Expectations formalize them.
careers.softwareEngineering: Collecting all validation errors at once is better UX and easier to test than failing on the first one.
careers.webDevelopment: This is what Pydantic and Django forms do for every request body: typed fields, defaults and error lists.
